scenes.headline: How Nanite's cluster hierarchy works in three.js
scenes.sub: Build it, cut it, and see what WebGL2 can't do
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Vertie. This is three-nanite. Let's build its hierarchy, then cut it.

steps.say: Take a few neighbouring clusters as a group. The vertices it shares with other groups are locked.

steps.term: Locked border: edges that may not move
steps.say: Merge them and simplify to half. The outer border cannot move, so it still meets its neighbours.
Split the result into half as many clusters, and repeat until one is left.

params.row: the hierarchy, coarsest row on top

steps.say: Here is a small hierarchy, the source clusters at the bottom, each row half the one below.

steps.term: Cut: one cluster for each piece of surface
steps.say: A cluster is drawn when its error, projected to pixels, is small enough, and its parent's is not.
Move the camera, and the cut follows it. Fine where the camera is close, coarse far away.
Now let each child measure its parent from its own bounds. Siblings disagree, and holes open.

scenes.title: Error, in pixels

parts.note: the group's error, scaled by the screen
parts.say: The group's error in mesh units, times a constant from the screen height and field of view.

parts.note: the nearest point the group could be
parts.say: Divided by the distance to the nearest point of its sphere. Siblings share that sphere, so they agree.

scenes.say: Every group carries one error and one sphere.

steps.say: The article's widget does the same thing. With the shared test, the curve never breaks.

steps.caption: own bounds: three holes
steps.say: Switch to own bounds, and three holes open at once.
Back to shared, and they close.
So I built the whole hierarchy in the page. Twenty-five rocks, each choosing its own cut. The colour is the level.

steps.caption: threshold up: coarser levels
steps.say: Raise the threshold, and every rock climbs to coarser levels, until only the top of the hierarchy is left.

scenes.title: Drawn at the starting view
scenes.say: Thirty-two million triangles in the scene. At one pixel, the cut draws about two hundred and twenty-eight thousand. My crack test found no open edges in any cut.

steps.say: Zoom in, and the clusters near the camera get small.

steps.caption: cut frozen, camera pulled back
steps.say: Freeze the cut and pull back. Only what was inside the old view was ever drawn.
What makes Nanite fast is the other half. Clusters of triangles under thirty-two pixels go to a compute rasteriser.
It writes depth and ids with one atomic, and shades each pixel once, afterwards.
Nanite streams pages of groups. three-nanite streams whole levels.
And it culls hidden clusters, not just hidden props. WebGL2 has no compute shaders, so none of this is there.

steps.caption: 1,791,044 at the peak
steps.say: So the win is drawing fewer triangles, not cheaper ones. Here the yellow number stays under two million.

scenes.text: The hierarchy and its cut work in WebGL2. Cheap pixel-sized triangles still need compute.
